extracted.intended_audience: general readers interested in media advocacy, television/content ratings, and media watchdog activity
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluative framework and practices used to judge television and other entertainment for suitability for family viewing, including a traffic-light rating system, content-analysis metrics, and advertiser/airtime considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Traffic light system (overall rating)
rubrics_metrics.description: A rating system in use since the 1995–96 season that evaluates broadcast TV programs across three categories (sex, violence, profanity) using a traffic-light metaphor and accumulates those category ratings into an overall rating.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Green = appropriate for all ages; Yellow = would be unsuitable for children under the age of 14; Red = appropriate for adult audiences only. The council has released annual 'best and worst prime-time television programs for family viewing' lists based on this system. Starting with the 2005–2006 season, their list was based on the traffic light system as well as Nielsen Media Research ratings of viewership among children ages 2–17.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sex (content dimension)
rubrics_metrics.description: One of three explicit content dimensions the PTC rates (sex) when assessing program suitability for families.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as a separate traffic-light category (green/yellow/red) contributing to an overall rating. The PTC objects to what it perceives as 'gratuitous' sexual content and evaluates both depiction and context (e.g., concerns about sexualization of minors, threesome scenes, simulated oral sex, exposure of nudity). Examples of targeted content include teen sexual scenes and performances the council deemed sexually explicit even if aired late.

rubrics_metrics.name: Violence (content dimension)
rubrics_metrics.description: One of three explicit content dimensions the PTC rates (violence) when assessing program suitability for families.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measured and reported (e.g., counts of violent incidents); used as a separate traffic-light category contributing to the overall rating. PTC has produced reports identifying programs/networks with high counts of violent incidents (e.g., naming Teen Titans as very violent in a 2005 study).

rubrics_metrics.name: Profanity (content dimension)
rubrics_metrics.description: One of three explicit content dimensions the PTC rates (profanity/language) when assessing program suitability for families.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PTC counts instances of foul language (e.g., reporting increases in prime-time profanity, counting occurrences within the Family Viewing Hour and across prime time) and flags programs/network broadcasts that include unbleeped profanity. Profanity ratings feed into the traffic-light category and overall score.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of child viewership data (Nielsen weighting)
rubrics_metrics.description: Since 2005–2006, the PTC has incorporated Nielsen Media Research ratings of child viewership (ages 2–17) into its seasonal 'best/worst' lists alongside its traffic light ratings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The PTC uses Nielsen viewership among children to help determine which programs matter most to family audiences; lists are based on both content ratings and youth viewership data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content-analysis by instance counts
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical method used in PTC reports: counting discrete instances of target content (e.g., profanity, violent incidents, depictions of violence against women) across programs, time periods, and seasons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include counting profanity occurrences during the 8pm-9pm 'Family Viewing Hour' and across prime time, reporting percent increases over time (e.g., comparisons between 2005 and 2010). The methodology has been criticized for misinterpretation (e.g., alleged misreading of satire in SpongeBob's 'Sailor Mouth'). PTC claims to support research with its Entertainment Tracking System archive of prime-time programming.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy and proper use of TV Parental Guidelines and content descriptors
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment criterion that compares broadcaster-applied TV Parental Guidelines (age-based ratings like TV-PG, TV-14 and content descriptors such as 'L' for language or 'V' for violence) against PTC's own assessments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PTC runs columns (e.g., 'So You Think You Can Rate a TV Show?') calling out networks for applying improper age-based ratings or omitting appropriate content descriptors; part of their evaluation is whether networks' self-ratings match independent content judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time-slot / safe-harbor suitability
rubrics_metrics.description: Consideration of whether potentially indecent content is aired during hours when children might be exposed (references to 'Family Viewing Hour' and FCC time frames).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PTC objects to broadcasts of explicit content during evening prime-time hours frequently viewed by children (it cites 8pm–9pm as the Family Viewing Hour and references the FCC's 6am–10pm safe-harbor window). Time-of-day is used to judge appropriateness and to trigger complaint campaigns when content airs before the safe times.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertising suitability for child audiences
rubrics_metrics.description: Criteria for evaluating television commercials' appropriateness when they are likely to be viewed by children.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PTC criticizes ads it deems sexually suggestive or 'soft-core porn' and objects when such ads air during programs likely watched by children. The council mobilizes members to contact advertisers and campaign for ad removal or sponsor accountability; examples include campaigns against Carl's Jr./Hardee's ads and biscuit-holes ad controversies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seal of Approval (recognition criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: An award PTC gives to television shows, movies, home products, and advertisers that 'provide or sponsor content it deems to be "family-friendly"'; divided into Entertainment and Advertiser categories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seal recipients are programs/products PTC considers family-friendly (examples provided: 7th Heaven, American Idol, Extreme Makeover: Home Edition, Disney properties). The Seal functions as positive recognition as opposed to the traffic-light/complaint-driven approach.
